resources.string: The game is in progress. Do you want to save it before quitting?
The game disappears from the list. Games already saved in the log are kept.
%1$s is played with %2$s. You entered %3$s: at least %4$d are needed. Go back to add more.
%1$s is played with %2$s. You entered %3$s: no more than %4$d are allowed. Go back to remove some.
Numbered rounds, one column per player (as before).
Each player has a total, with +1/-1 buttons. No rounds.
Each round, you choose who is on which team (e.g. French Tarot with a called partner).
Like Skyjo, instead of the highest
E.g. for Tarot: \"Garde\" ×2. E.g. for Belote: \"Capot\" ×1 +250. A selector will then let you choose the rule to apply.
As soon as the threshold is crossed
At the end of the current round
Deciding round if tied for the lead
Plays another round if several players are tied at the top
Points ahead of every opponent required to finish (2 in table tennis). Empty: no lead required.
As soon as a player reaches this score, the game ends even without the required lead (30 in badminton). Empty: no cap.
Leave empty to allow 1 to 12 players.
Each player fills each line once, like in Yahtzee. The game ends when every box is filled.
Each round, you enter the bid and the tricks won: the score is worked out for you.
You must reach the target score exactly. Go over it and you drop back to the fallback score (like Mölkky).
Start from a score and count down to exactly 0. A turn that goes below 0 or stops at 1 is cancelled (like darts).
Each round: taker, contract, oudlers and points. Score, bonuses and slam are calculated. For 3 to 5 players.
13 categories, with a 35-point bonus from 63 in the upper section.
4 colours (points depend on the number of crosses) and penalties.
10 frames, roll by roll: strikes and spares are counted automatically.
One category per line. To offer score buttons, add “:” then the values separated by commas (e.g. Coins: 0, 1, 2, 3). Without values, the score is typed on the keyboard.
Add at least one category, otherwise the game will be a regular rounds table.
20 points + 10 per bid trick if the bid is exact, otherwise −10 per trick of difference.
10 points + 1 per bid trick if the bid is exact, otherwise −1 per trick of difference.
Each player moves up phase by phase (like Phase 10). The ranking takes the phase reached into account.
The end of the game is handled by the chosen mechanic.
The loser is eliminated. Semi-finals, final and third-place match are generated automatically.
Everyone plays everyone, and the standings are based on wins. %1$d participants at most.
Participants play in the order entered: 1st against 2nd, 3rd against 4th… If there are not enough players to fill the bracket, the last ones in the list advance automatically.
Tap the winner’s name for each match: the standings update by themselves. A mistake? “Fix” cancels the result.
Tap the winner’s name for each match. A mistake? “Fix” cancels the result.
The matches of the following rounds that were already played will be cancelled and must be replayed.
The current tournament is not finished: it will be erased.
For each game, the last %1$d plays are kept.
No saved games yet. Use the \"Save\" button during a game to find it here.
The finished games (%1$d) will be deleted. Games in progress are kept.
This file is not a My Scores backup.
This backup comes from a newer version of the app: update the app to import it.
Based on %1$s from the log%2$s. The log keeps the last %3$d plays of each game.
No finished games in the log yet. Statistics are built from finished, saved games.
No finished games in the log yet. Statistics are built from finished, saved games (games in progress do not count yet).
Writes a small code (A, B, C…) on each colour
Who takes this round? (taker, or taker + called partner)
Change the sign of the score
The selected team gets this score, and all the other players get the opposite.
Points made by the taker (0 to 91)
Petit au bout (Petit in the last trick)
The defence did not win every trick
Defence slam: +%1$d for the defenders (house rule)
A successful slam is added automatically at 91 points.
Free game: the app is simply a scoresheet for any game.
Each player has a column. Each round, write down the points scored. The highest total leads the standings.
Tap a cell to enter a score. A new round is added automatically. The game never ends by itself.
Have as few points as possible when a player reaches or exceeds 100 points.

• 150 cards worth from −2 to 12.
• Each player gets 12 cards face down, in a grid of 3 rows × 4 columns.
• Everyone flips 2 cards of their grid. The player with the highest total starts.
• One card is turned over to start the discard pile.

• Draw a card, or take the visible card from the discard pile.
• Drawn card: swap it with a card in your grid (face up or face down), or discard it and flip a face-down card.
• Card from the discard pile: you must swap it with a card in your grid.
• If a column shows 3 identical cards, it is discarded.

As soon as a player has all their cards face up, the others play one last turn. Everyone then adds up their cards. If the player who finished does not have the strictly lowest score of the round, their score is doubled (if it is positive).
Enter each player’s score every round (+/− button for negatives). The standings favour the lowest total. The game ends at the end of the round in which a player reaches 100 points.
The taker (alone, or with a partner in 5-player games) must fulfil the announced contract against the defenders. Played by 3 to 5 players, most often 4.

78 cards: 56 suit cards, 21 trumps and the Excuse. The 3 oudlers are the trump 1 (the Petit), the 21 and the Excuse. Values: King 4.5 · Queen 3.5 · Knight 2.5 · Jack 1.5 · oudler 4.5 · other cards 0.5 (91 points in all).

• Petite (×1): the taker takes the dog, then discards the same number of cards.
• Garde (×2): like the petite, with a higher stake.
• Garde sans le chien (×4): the dog stays with the taker without being used.
• Garde contre le chien (×6): the dog goes to the defenders.
Depending on the taker’s number of oudlers: 0 oudlers = 56 points · 1 oudler = 51 · 2 oudlers = 41 · 3 oudlers = 36.

Base score = 25 + the difference between the points made and the contract. It is positive if the contract is made, negative if it fails. It is multiplied by the bid’s multiplier.
• Petit au bout: ±10, multiplied by the multiplier (+ for the taker, − for the defence).
• Handful (Poignée): single 20 · double 30 · triple 40, won by the side that wins the round (not multiplied).
• Slam (all tricks): +200 unannounced · +400 announced and made · −200 announced and failed (not multiplied).
• Defence slam: +200 for the defenders (house rule, not in the official rules).
The score obtained is paid by each defender to the taker (and to the partner in 5-player games).

For each round, choose the taker (and the called partner in 5-player games), the contract, the number of oudlers and the points made, then tick any bonuses. At 91 points, a successful slam is added automatically. The app calculates each player’s score (the sum of the round is always zero) and shows it before you confirm. The pencil in the history lets you correct a round.
Played by 4 in 2 teams with 32 cards. One team chooses a trump suit and must score more points than the opponents. The game is played over several rounds up to the target score.

• Trump suit: Jack 20 · 9 14 · Ace 11 · 10 10 · King 4 · Queen 3 · 8 and 7: 0.\n• Other suits: Ace 11 · 10 10 · King 4 · Queen 3 · Jack 2 · 9, 8, 7: 0.\n• Dix de der (last trick): +10. Total for a round: 162 points.
Each player gets 8 cards. The taker chooses the trump suit. 8 tricks are played; you must follow suit, otherwise trump or overtrump.

• Belote-rebelote (King + Queen of trumps): +20.
• The taker must make at least 82 points. Otherwise it is “dedans” (failed): the opponent scores 162 points.
• Capot (all tricks): 252 points.
• Declarations (tierce, fifty, hundred, four of a kind) exist depending on the variant.
Enter the points of each round. The game ends at the end of the round in which a player or team reaches 501 points.
Be the first to get rid of all your cards, and finish the game with as few points as possible.

• On your turn, draw (from the stock or the discard pile), you may lay down melds, then discard a card.
• Melds: runs of at least 3 cards of the same suit, or sets of three or four of a kind of different suits.
• The joker replaces any card.
• The first meld must reach a minimum number of points, agreed before playing (variants differ).

The player who “goes out” (no more cards in hand) scores 0. The others count the cards left in their hand: numbered cards = their value, face cards = 10, Ace and joker depending on the chosen variant.
Enter each player’s points every round. The lowest total wins and the game ends at the end of the round in which a player reaches 500 points.
Be the first to play all your cards.

• Each player gets 7 cards. One card is turned over to start the discard pile.
• Play a card of the same colour, the same number or the same symbol.
• With no playable card, draw one card.
• Special cards: +2, reverse, skip, wild, wild +4.
• You must say “UNO” before playing your second-to-last card, otherwise you draw 2 penalty cards.
The winner of the round scores the points of the cards left in the other players’ hands: numbered cards = their value · +2, reverse, skip = 20 · wild and wild +4 = 50.
Enter the points won by each player every round. The highest score leads. The game does not end automatically (the official rule sets the target at 500 points).

Fill the 13 categories of the sheet while scoring as many points as possible. Each category is played only once per player. The game ends when all the cells of all the players are filled: the highest total wins.

On your turn, roll 5 dice up to 3 times, keeping the dice of your choice between rolls. Then write the result in a category that is still free. If no combination fits, you must “cross out” a category: it is then worth 0 points.

Aces, Twos, Threes, Fours, Fives, Sixes: add up only the dice showing that number (three 4s give 12 in “Fours”). If the upper section total reaches 63 or more, you get a 35-point bonus: the app adds it automatically.

Three of a kind: at least 3 identical dice, you score the sum of the 5 dice. Four of a kind: at least 4 identical dice, sum of the 5 dice. Full house: 3 identical dice and a pair, 25 points. Small straight: 4 consecutive dice, 30 points. Large straight: 5 consecutive dice, 40 points. Yams: 5 identical dice, 50 points. Chance: sum of the 5 dice, no condition.

Tap a cell to enter the category’s score. For fixed-value categories, tap the value directly, or “Cross out” to enter 0. For Three of a kind, Four of a kind and Chance, type the sum of the dice. The fixed values (25 / 30 / 40 / 50) vary slightly between households: these are the classic Yams ones.
Avoid collecting tokens. Each round, the loser takes some; at the end of the game, the player with the fewest wins. The app counts each player’s tokens with the +1 and −1 buttons.
On your turn, roll 3 dice up to 3 times, keeping the dice you want. The first player of the round decides how many rolls everyone else is allowed. The best hand wins the round, the worst loses it.

From best to worst: 421 (10 tokens), 111 (7 tokens), a pair of aces with another die such as 116 (as many tokens as the third die), then the three of a kind 666 (6 tokens), 555 (5), 444 (4), 333 (3), 222 (2), then the straights 456, 345, 234, 123 (2 tokens each). All other hands are worth 1 token.

You start with 21 tokens in the middle: this is the “charge”. The loser of each round takes from the middle as many tokens as the winner’s hand is worth. When there are no more tokens in the middle, the “discharge” begins: the loser of the round then takes tokens from the winner. The player who ends up with all the tokens at the end of the discharge loses the game. The exact rules vary a lot from one household to another.
Each player has a token counter. Add tokens to the loser of the round and, during the discharge, remove some from the winner. The standings put the player with the fewest first.
Reach or exceed 343 points (the letters C, D, C are the 3rd, 4th and 3rd letters of the alphabet). The app stops the game as soon as a player reaches this score.
On your turn, roll two dice (the “chouettes”), then a third one (the “cul”). Depending on the combination, you score points, or lose some.

Chouette: two identical dice, you score the square of their value (two 5s give 25 points). Velute: one die equals the sum of the other two, you score 2 times the square of that die (2-3-5 gives 50 points). Chouette-velute: a chouette that is also a velute (1-1-2, for example); it is worth the velute, but only the first player to clap their hands while shouting “Pas mou le caillou!” scores these points. Cul de chouette: three identical dice, 40 points plus 10 times the value of the die (from 50 to 100 points). Suite (straight): three consecutive dice (3-4-5, for example); the last player to react loses points, often 10, depending on the variants. Néant: no combination, nothing happens.

A player who rolls a néant wins a Grelottine. It lets them challenge another player who has just rolled a néant: they choose a combination the challenged player must make and bet part of their score (at most about 30% of the lower of the two scores). If the challenged player succeeds, they win the stake; otherwise, they lose it to the challenger.

Each row of the table corresponds to a roll: enter the points won or lost in the column of the player who rolled. The + / − button lets you enter a negative score (suite lost, Grelottine stake lost). The game stops as soon as a player reaches 343.
Be the first to reach 10,000 points. When a player gets there, the others play one last turn: the app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

Roll 6 dice. After each roll, set aside at least one scoring die, then either roll the remaining dice again or stop to keep the turn’s points. If a roll scores no points (a “Farkle”), you lose all the turn’s points. If all 6 dice have scored, you may roll all of them again.

A 1 is worth 100 points, a 5 is worth 50. Three identical dice are worth 100 times their value (three 4s: 400 points), except three 1s which are worth 1,000. A straight from 1 to 6 and three pairs are often worth 1,500. The exact values and the opening rule (for example 500 points minimum to start scoring) vary between households.
Each turn, enter in the player’s column the points they kept (0 if they rolled a Farkle).
Be the first to reach 100 points. The app stops the game as soon as a player gets there.

Roll one die as many times as you like and add the results to the turn total. If you roll a 1, the turn ends and you lose the turn total. You may also stop earlier: the turn total is then added to your score.
At the end of each turn, enter in the player’s column the points kept (0 if the player rolled a 1). The variant with pigs to throw (Pass the Pigs) is played the same way.
Be the first to eat 13 brains. When a player gets there, the others finish the round. If there is a tie for the lead, an extra round decides between the players (the app offers it).

Draw 3 dice from the cup and roll them. A brain is kept, a shotgun blast is to be avoided, and footprints force you to re-roll that die. You can stop to keep your brains or carry on by drawing more dice. With 3 shotgun blasts, the turn is lost and you lose the turn’s brains.
13 dice: 6 green (easy: 3 brains, 2 footprints, 1 shotgun), 4 yellow (2 brains, 2 footprints, 2 shotguns) and 3 red (dangerous: 1 brain, 2 footprints, 3 shotguns).
At the end of each turn, enter in the player’s column the number of brains eaten (0 if they lost their turn).
Shut all the flaps of the box (numbered 1 to 9) or, failing that, leave as few open as possible. The lowest total over the agreed number of rounds wins.
Roll the 2 dice and shut one or more flaps whose sum equals the total of the dice. Keep going until you can no longer shut a flap. When flaps 7, 8 and 9 are shut, you may roll just one die.
The turn’s score is the sum of the flaps left open. Shutting everything gives 0: this is “shutting the box”.

Each round, enter in the player’s column the sum of the flaps left open (0 if the box is shut). The app does not end the game: agree on the number of rounds to play (5, for example) and look at the standings.
Score the most points over 6 rounds. In round 1, you look for 1s; in round 2, for 2s; and so on up to round 6.

Roll 3 dice. Each die showing the round’s number scores 1 point. Three dice of the round’s number are a “Bunco” and score 21 points. Three identical dice of another number score 5 points. As long as you score, you may keep rolling.
Each round, enter in the player’s column the points scored during their turn. The app does not end the game: after the 6 rounds, the highest total wins.
Be the first monster to reach 20 victory points, or the last monster still alive. The app counts everyone’s victory points and stops the game at 20.

Roll 6 dice up to 3 times, keeping the dice you want. Three identical dice of value 1, 2 or 3 score 1, 2 or 3 points (each extra identical die adds 1 point). A heart heals (not possible in Tokyo), a lightning bolt gives energy, a claw attacks the other monsters.
Entering Tokyo scores 1 point; starting your turn in Tokyo scores 2. The monster in Tokyo attacks all the others, but all of them can attack it.
Add (+1 / −1) each monster’s victory points. Health points and energy are tracked on the game boards.
Do not lose all your lives: the last player who still has some wins. The app counts the lives lost by each player.
Each player rolls 2 dice, up to 3 times, hiding the result or showing it depending on the variant. The first player sets the number of rolls allowed. The worst hand of the round loses a life.

From best to worst: Mexico (2 and 1), then the doubles from 6-6 down to 1-1, then the other hands, reading the higher die first (6-5 beats 6-4, which beats 5-4, etc.). The exact rules vary from one household to another.

Add 1 to the counter of the player who loses the round. Agree on the number of lives lost that eliminates a player (5, for example). The app does not end the game; the standings put the player who has lost the fewest lives first.
Tick as many numbers as possible in each of the 4 colours, to score the most points. The game ends when two rows are closed with a lock, or when a player has 4 penalties.

The active player rolls all 6 dice (2 white and 4 coloured). All players may tick the sum of the two white dice in the colour of their choice. Then the active player may tick the sum of one white die and one coloured die, in the colour of that die. You always tick from left to right, without going back. An active player who ticks nothing takes a penalty.

The red and yellow rows go from 2 to 12, the green and blue rows from 12 to 2. To close a row, you must already have at least 5 crosses in it and tick the last number: you also tick the lock, which counts as one more cross.
For each colour: 1 cross = 1 point, 2 crosses = 3 points, 3 crosses = 6 points, and so on (1 + 2 + 3 +…), up to 78 points for 12 crosses. Each penalty costs 5 points.
At the end of the game, tap the cell of each colour to choose the points matching the number of crosses, then the penalties cell. The game is over when all the cells are filled.
A Belote variant played by 4, in two teams, with bidding. The first team to reach 1,000 points wins (some tables play to 2,000). The app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

Each player in turn announces a contract (from 80 to 160 points, or capot) in a suit, or passes. The highest contract wins and the team that announced it must make it. A player on the opposing team may “coinche” (double): all the points of the deal are then doubled. The team that had bid may “surcoinche” (redouble) to quadruple them.

There are 162 points per deal (152 card points and 10 points for the last trick), plus 20 points if a team has belote-rebelote. Contract made: the team that took scores its trick points and its contract, the opposing team scores its own. Contract failed: the opposing team scores 160 points, plus the contract. If the contract was doubled, the result of the team that wins the deal is multiplied by 2 (doubled) or 4 (redoubled). Scoring rules vary between tables.
Each deal, enter in each team’s column the points scored. Tap the multiplier under the cell to choose Doubled (×2) or Redoubled (×4). You can play with 2 columns (“Us” and “Them”) or 4 players.

Get rid of all your cards as fast as possible. At the end of each round, the players are ranked: the first is the President, the last is the Scum (or “Trou”). There is no fixed end: it is up to you to decide when to stop.

Cards are played in turn, always laying the same number of cards of equal or higher value than the ones laid before. Anyone who cannot or does not want to play passes. The last player to have laid cards collects the trick and starts again. The 2 is the highest card.
In the next round, the Scum gives their best cards to the President, who gives back their worst ones (2 cards; 1 card for the vice-president and the vice-scum).
A suggested set of points to track the standings: President +2, Vice-president +1, neutrals 0, Vice-scum −1, Scum −2. Adapt it to your table.
After each round, enter in each player’s column the points matching their place (negative scores allowed with the +/− button). The standings put the highest total first.

Collect as few points as possible. Each deal, every heart collected is worth 1 point and the queen of spades 13 points. The game ends when a player reaches 100 points: the player with the fewest wins. The app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

With 4 players and a 52-card deck, everyone passes 3 cards to a neighbour (left, right, across, then no passing, depending on the hand). The player with the 2 of clubs starts. You follow suit if you can; whoever has the highest card of that suit wins the trick. You cannot lead a heart until a heart has been discarded, unless you only have hearts.

A player who collects all the hearts and the queen of spades (26 points) “shoots the moon”: they score 0 and each of the other players scores 26 points (or, depending on the table, they subtract 26 points from their own score).
After each deal, enter in each player’s column the points collected. The game is played by 3 to 6 players (the rules above are those for 4).

Make the number of tricks you bid. The teams (2 against 2) score points by making their contract; the first team to reach 500 points wins. The app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

With a 52-card deck, spades are always trump. Each player announces the number of tricks they expect to take; the team’s bids are added together. All players must follow suit if possible. You cannot lead a spade until a spade has been played, unless you only have spades.

Contract made: 10 points per bid trick, plus 1 point per extra trick (a “bag”). Contract failed: you lose 10 points per bid trick. A successful zero-trick bid (“nil”) scores 100 points; a failed one loses 100. Each team that accumulates 10 bags loses 100 points.
At the end of each deal, enter in each team’s column the points won or lost (the +/− button lets you enter a negative score). You can play with 2 columns (the two teams) or 4 players.

Make melds (sets and runs of the same suit) with the 10 cards of your hand, leaving as few points as possible in unmatched cards (the “deadwood”). The first person to reach 100 points wins. The app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

On your turn, draw a card (from the stock or the discard pile) then discard one. When the total of your unmatched cards is 10 points or less, you may “knock” to end the deal. Ace = 1 point, face cards = 10 points, other cards = their value.

The player who knocks scores the difference between the opponent’s unmatched cards and their own. If they have no unmatched cards (“gin”), they also score 25 points. If the opponent has as many points or fewer, it is an “undercut”: the opponent scores the difference plus 25 points. At the end of the game, the winner adds 100 points, plus 25 per deal won.
After each deal, enter the points scored in the column of the deal’s winner (0 for the other player). The game is played by 2.

Get rid of all your cards before the others. During the game, the points left in each player’s hand are added to their score: when a player reaches 100 points, the game stops and the player with the fewest points wins. The app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

Everyone gets 5 cards (7 with two players). On your turn, play a card of the same suit or the same value as the last card played. The 8s are wild: you can play them at any time and choose the suit that follows. When you cannot play, you draw.
When a player has no cards left, the others count the points in their hand: 8 = 50 points, face cards = 10 points, ace = 1 point, other cards = their value. Some tables play to 200 points.
At the end of each deal, enter in each player’s column the points in their hand (0 for the one who won the deal). The standings put the lowest total first.
Be the first to reach 121 points, scoring them on the board. The app stops the game as soon as a player reaches 121.

Each player gets 6 cards (5 with three players) and sets 2 aside in the “crib”, an extra hand that goes to the dealer. One card is turned up (the “starter”). The cards are then played in turn while announcing the running total (“pegging”), without going over 31, and then each hand is counted.

Fifteen (cards adding up to 15): 2 points. Pair: 2 points; three of a kind: 6 points; four of a kind: 12 points. Run of 3 cards or more: 1 point per card. Flush: 4 points for 4 cards of the same suit in the hand, 5 if the starter is also of that suit. Jack of the same suit as the starter (“nobs”): 1 point. Face cards = 10 points, ace = 1 point.
In each player’s column, enter the points scored in each phase (pegging, hand, crib) as a row of the table.

Travel 1,000 kilometres before the other teams, by playing distance cards and hindering your opponents. A game is played over several deals: the first team to reach 5,000 points in total wins. The app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

Draw a card, then play one or discard one. To move forward, you first need a green light. Hazards (accident, out of gas, flat tyre, speed limit, red light) block the opponents; remedies unblock them; safeties (driving ace, extra tank, puncture-proof, right of way) protect against them forever. You may not go over 1,000 kilometres.

Each kilometre travelled is worth 1 point. Bonuses: 100 points per safety played (300 more for all four); 300 points per coup fourré (immediate remedy to a hazard thanks to the matching safety); 400 points for a completed trip (1,000 km); 300 points if the trip is completed after the end of the stock (“delayed action”), or without having played a 200 km card (“safe trip”), or if the team played the extension to 1,000 km (200 points); 500 points if the opposing team has laid no kilometre (“shut-out”). You can play in teams of 2 by entering two “players”.
At the end of each deal, enter in each team’s column its points (distance and bonuses). The exact bonus values vary by edition: adapt them to the rules of your box.
Collect as few bull heads as possible. The game ends when a player reaches 66 bull heads (or more): the player with the fewest wins. The app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

The 104 cards are numbered from 1 to 104. Everyone gets 10 cards and 4 cards are placed in rows on the table. Each turn, all players secretly choose a card and reveal it together. Starting with the lowest, each card is placed at the end of the row whose last card is the closest below it. If the card is lower than all the row-end cards, the player chooses a row to pick up.

The player who places the 6th card of a row picks up the other 5 cards, and their bull heads. Each card is worth 1 bull head, except: multiples of 5 (2 heads), multiples of 10 (3 heads), multiples of 11 (5 heads) and 55 (7 heads).
At the end of each round (10 turns), enter in each player’s column the number of bull heads collected. The standings put the lowest total first.

Collect as few points as possible. Each round, every Payoo card collected is worth the number of points written on it, and the Papayoo (the 7 of the suit chosen by the die) is worth 40 points. Games are played over as many rounds as there are players: the lowest total wins.

At the start of each round, each player passes a few cards to their neighbour, then a die chooses the Papayoo’s suit. Play then goes as in Belote, with no trump: you follow suit if you can, and the highest card takes the trick.

At the end of each round, enter in each player’s column the points collected. The app does not end the game: it is up to you to stop after as many rounds as there are players. The details of the cards and the number of cards passed depend on the box: check the rules of your copy.
Have the lowest sum of cards in hand at the end of each round. The game ends when a player goes over 100 points (the app stops at 101 and above): the player with the fewest points wins.

Each player has 4 cards in front of them, which they do not look at (except two at the start). On your turn, draw a card, then either keep it in exchange for one of yours or discard it. Some discarded cards let you look at a card, or swap cards with an opponent. When a player thinks they have the lowest hand, they say “Cabo”: everyone plays one more turn, then the cards are revealed.

Add up the value of each player’s cards (the values are written on the cards). The player who said Cabo scores 0 if they have the lowest hand, otherwise they score their sum plus a 10-point penalty. The others score their sum. If a player reaches exactly 100 points, their score drops back to 50 (rule from the box).
At the end of each round, enter each player’s sum in their column. If a player reaches exactly 100, fix their cell to bring it back to 50.
Enter both numbers to calculate the score.

A trick-taking game for 4 players, in two teams of 2, with a 32-card deck. Each team tries to collect the most card points. The game is often played to 101 points: the app finishes the current round, then announces the winner. The rules vary a lot between regions: adapt them to your table.

The order of the cards is: 10 (the “manille”), ace (the “manillon”), king, queen, jack, 9, 8, 7. Card points: manille 5, manillon 4, king 3, queen 2, jack 1, the 9, 8 and 7 are worth nothing. There are 60 card points in the deck (variants add points for the last trick).

Everyone gets 8 cards. After the trump suit has been turned up or chosen, tricks are played: you must follow suit if you can, otherwise trump if you have a trump. The team that wins a trick collects the cards and their points.
In Manille coinchée, a team may “double” the opposing contract to double the points of the deal, and the other may “redouble” to quadruple them.
Each deal, enter in each team’s column the points scored. Tap the multiplier under the cell to choose Doubled (×2) or Redoubled (×4). You can play with 2 columns (the two teams) or 4 players.

An Italian game played with a 40-card deck (remove the 8s, 9s and 10s from a 52-card deck, or use an Italian deck). The first player to reach 11 points wins; some tables play to 21. If there is a tie for the lead, an extra deal is played.

Everyone gets 3 cards and 4 cards are placed on the table. On your turn, you play a card from your hand: it captures a card of the same value or several cards whose sum equals its value. If you cannot capture anything, the card stays on the table. When a card clears the table, you score a “scopa”.

At the end of each deal, you score 1 point for each of: most cards, most diamonds (coins), the 7 of diamonds (“settebello”), the best “primiera” (best combination of 4 cards of different suits), and 1 point for each scopa made.
At the end of each deal, enter in each player’s column the points of the deal (scopas included). They are added to their total.
Finish each round with the fewest points in hand. The game ends when a player goes over 200 points (the app stops at 201 and above): the player with the fewest points wins.

With a 54-card deck (jokers = 0 points, ace = 1, face cards = 10, other cards = their value), each player gets 5 cards. On your turn, discard a card, a pair, a three of a kind or a run of at least 3 cards of the same suit, then draw a card (from the stock or the last discard). When you have 5 points or less in hand, you may call “Yaniv” at the start of your turn.

After a “Yaniv”, everyone counts their cards. If nobody has as many points or fewer than the player who called, they score 0 and the others score the total of their hand. If another player has as many or fewer (“Assaf”), the player who called scores the total of their hand plus 30 points, and the player with the fewest scores 0. Depending on the rules, a score of exactly 100 or 200 is halved.
At the end of each round, enter in each player’s column the points scored. If a player reaches exactly 100 or 200 points and your rule halves it, fix their cell by hand.

A trick-taking game with penalties (most often for 4 players, with 52 cards). Each player, when it is their turn to deal, chooses one contract out of seven, once each. The highest total wins at the end of the game (there is no automatic end).

No tricks: −2 per trick collected. No hearts: −5 per heart collected. No queens: −10 per queen collected. No king of hearts: −20 for whoever collects it (the “Barbu”). No last trick: −40 for whoever takes the last trick. Salad: all these penalties at once. Domino: you lay your cards like dominoes, and the ranking gives points or penalties depending on the order in which players empty their hands.
At the end of each deal, enter in each player’s column their points (the +/− button lets you enter a negative score). The contract values vary between tables: adapt them to yours.

Win exactly the number of tricks you bid, no more and no less. With 52 cards, the number of cards dealt goes up from 1 to the maximum possible, then back down. The game has no automatic end: play all the planned rounds.

Each player gets n cards and a card is turned up to choose the trump suit. In turn, each player announces the number of tricks they expect to win (the dealer often cannot bid a number that would make the total of the bids equal the number of tricks). The tricks are then played, and you must follow suit.
Bid made: 10 points plus the number of tricks bid. Bid missed: you lose one point per trick of difference from your bid. These values vary between tables.
Each round, tap a player’s cell and enter their tricks bid and tricks won: the app calculates the round’s score and adds it to their total.

Get rid of all your tiles by laying them on the table in runs and groups. At the end of each round, the winner scores the sum of the tiles left to the other players, and each loser loses the value of their tiles. There is no automatic end: decide on the number of rounds.

Everyone starts with 14 tiles. The first meld must be worth at least 30 points. After that, you may lay down new combinations or rearrange those on the table. A run has at least 3 consecutive tiles of the same colour; a group has 3 or 4 tiles of the same value and different colours. If you cannot play, you draw a tile.
Each tile is worth its number. A joker left in hand is worth 30 points against the player who keeps it. The winner of a round scores the sum of the values of all the other players’ tiles.
At the end of each round, enter in each loser’s column the total of their tiles as a negative number (+/− button), and in the winner’s column the sum of the points lost by the others.

Be the first to get rid of all your dominoes. At the end of each round, the winner scores the sum of the points left in the other players’ hands. The first player to reach 100 points wins (some tables play to 200). The app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

With a set of 28 dominoes (double-six), each player gets 7 with two players, or 5 with three or four players; the rest form the boneyard. On your turn, lay a domino with one side matching an end of the chain. If you cannot play, you draw (or pass when the boneyard is empty).

When a player has laid all their dominoes, they score the sum of the points of the dominoes left to the others. If the game is blocked, the player with the fewest points in hand scores the difference with the others (depending on the variants).
At the end of each round, enter the points scored in the winner’s column (0 for the other players).

Announce exactly the number of tricks you will win. With a 60-card deck (52 cards, 4 Wizards and 4 Jesters), the number of rounds equals 60 divided by the number of players (20 rounds with 3 players): in round n, everyone gets n cards. The app does not stop the game: play all the planned rounds.

A card is turned up to choose the trump suit. In turn, each player announces the number of tricks they expect to win. The tricks are played by following the suit led. A Wizard always wins the trick (the first one played wins); a Jester always loses, unless it is alone.
Exact bid: 20 points plus 10 points per bid trick. Missed bid: −10 points per trick of difference.
Each round, tap a player’s cell and enter their tricks bid and tricks won: the app calculates the round’s score (positive or negative) and adds it to their total.

Complete the 10 phases of the game before the others, in order. Each round, each player tries to complete their current phase; those who do not stay on the same phase in the next round. The game ends when a player has completed phase 10. The app tracks each player’s phase in the “Phase” row at the bottom of the table.

1: 2 sets of 3. 2: 1 set of 3 and 1 run of 4. 3: 1 set of 4 and 1 run of 4. 4: 1 run of 7. 5: 1 run of 8. 6: 1 run of 9. 7: 2 sets of 4. 8: 7 cards of one colour. 9: 1 set of 5 cards of the same value and 1 pair. 10: 1 set of 5 cards of the same value and 1 set of 3.

When a player gets rid of all their cards, the others score the points of the cards left in their hands: cards 1 to 9 = 5 points, cards 10 to 12 = 10 points, Skip = 15 points, Wild = 25 points. The player with the fewest points ranks higher when phases are equal.

At the end of each round, enter each player’s points and update their phase by tapping the “Phase” row cell: choose ✓ for phase 10 completed. The standings are based first on the phase reached, then on points.
Tap the number of pins knocked down on each roll.

Be the first to reach 15 prestige points. When a player gets there, the current round is completed so that everyone has played the same number of turns, then the app announces the winner. In case of a tie, the player who bought the fewest development cards wins (to check by hand).

On your turn, a player takes a single action: take 3 gem tokens of different colours, take 2 tokens of the same colour, reserve a card (and take a gold token), or buy a development card, using their tokens and the bonuses from their cards. Cards give prestige points, and nobles visit those who have enough cards of a colour.
Each turn, add in the player’s column the prestige points gained (cards bought, nobles received).
Be the first to reach 30 points. The app finishes the current round, then announces the winner.

The storyteller chooses a card from their hand and gives a clue. The other players choose from their hand the card that fits best, then all the cards are shuffled and revealed, and everyone votes for the storyteller’s card.

If everyone or nobody found the storyteller’s card: the storyteller scores 0 and each of the others scores 2. Otherwise, the storyteller and those who found their card score 3. Each vote received by a player’s own card gives them 1 point if they are not the storyteller (3 points maximum).
Each turn, enter in each player’s column the points won.

Score the most points by laying trains on routes, completing destination tickets and building the longest line. Points are mostly counted at the end of the game, which ends when a player has almost no trains left.

Each route gives points according to its length: 1 train = 1 point, 2 = 2, 3 = 4, 4 = 7, 5 = 10, 6 = 15 (values from the “Europe” or “USA” version). Each completed ticket adds the points written on it, and each failed ticket subtracts them. The longest path bonus is 10 points. Unused stations in the Europe version are worth 4 points each.
Add the points in the player’s column as the game goes on, or the whole end of game at once (completed tickets as positive, failed tickets as negative with the +/− button for the row concerned).
Place tiles on your board in patterns to score the most points. The game ends after the round in which a player has completed a horizontal row of their wall.

During the game, each tile placed scores 1 point per tile in the same row and the same column that touch it. Tiles that fall on the floor lose 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3 then 3 points. At the end of the game, each complete row scores 2 points, each complete column 7 points, and each complete colour (5 tiles placed) 10 points.
Each round, add the score of the player’s board (positive or negative), then the end-of-game bonuses on a last row.
Lay tiles to build the landscape and place followers on it, in order to score the most points. The game ends when there are no more tiles.

Completed road: 1 point per tile. Completed city: 2 points per tile and per pennant. Completed monastery: 9 points (the monastery and its 8 neighbouring tiles). Farm at the end of the game: 3 points per adjacent completed city. At the end of the game, unfinished roads and cities score 1 point per tile (and per pennant), or 1 point per tile for a monastery.
Each time, enter in the column of the player concerned the points scored (one row per completed construction, or per turn).
Be the first player to reach 10 victory points during their turn. The app stops the game as soon as a player reaches 10 points.
Each settlement is worth 1 point, each city 2 points, the longest road (at least 5 segments) 2 points, the largest army (at least 3 knights) 2 points, and each victory point development card 1 point.
Add (+1 / −1) each player’s victory points as the game goes on: tap + twice for a city, and remove points when a player loses the longest road or the largest army.
Make your city prosper over three ages, then count the victory points at the end of the third age. The highest total wins.

Add up: military conflict points (victory and defeat tokens), coins (1 point per group of 3 coins), the wonder stages, civil buildings (blue), scientific buildings (green), commercial buildings (yellow) and guilds (purple). Each identical science symbol is worth the square of the number of symbols of that type, and each set of three different symbols is worth 7 more points.
At the end of the game, enter in each player’s column the total of each family of points, one family per row.
Place words on the board to score the most points. The game ends when the bag is empty and a player has played all their letters, or when nobody can play anymore. There is no automatic end.

Each letter is worth the number of points written on it. Double or triple letter squares multiply the value of a letter, double or triple word squares multiply the whole word. Playing all the letters of your rack in one move (a “bingo”) scores 50 extra points (or 50 instead of 40 depending on the rules). At the end of the game, each player loses the value of the letters they have left, and the player who finished gains them.
After each word placed, enter in the player’s column the points scored (one row per turn). At the end of the game, add a row with the remaining letters as a negative number (+/− button).

Win the 6 wedges, one per category, then answer the final question correctly. The app counts each player’s wedges and stops at 6: the final question, chosen by the other players, then remains to be answered.
Roll the die and move your token. The colour of the square you land on indicates the question’s category. A correct answer lets you roll again; on a wedge square, it also earns the category’s wedge.
Add (+1) a wedge to the player who has just won it.
Be the first team to reach 13 points. The app stops the game as soon as a team reaches 13.
Each team throws its boules to get as close as possible to the jack. At the end of the end, the team whose boule is closest scores 1 point for each of its boules closer than the best opposing boule.
Each end, enter in the column of the team that scored the points of the end (0 for the other team). You can play with 2 columns (the two teams) or head to head.
Reach exactly 50 points. If you go over 50, your score drops back to 25. The app applies this rule by itself and stops the game as soon as a player is at 50.

Players take turns throwing a wooden pin (the “mölkky”) at 12 skittles numbered from 1 to 12, from 3 or 4 metres. If a single skittle falls, you score its number. If several skittles fall, you score their count (3 skittles down = 3 points). The skittles are stood back up where they fell.
A player who misses all the skittles 3 times in a row is eliminated (to handle by hand: just stop entering points for them).
For each throw, enter in the player’s column the points scored. The total shown takes into account the drop back to 25 when going over.
Reach exactly 0 before the other players, starting from 301 points. The app stops the game as soon as a player is at 0.

On their turn, a player throws 3 darts and subtracts the total of their points from the remaining score. The last dart must usually land in a double (“double out”) to finish at 0. If a turn would take you below 0, or leave 1 point (impossible to finish on a double), the turn is cancelled and the score stays what it was.
Each turn, enter in the player’s column the total of their 3 darts. The app shows the remaining score, and automatically ignores a turn that would go below 0 or to 1.
Reach exactly 0 before the other players, starting from 501 points. The app stops the game as soon as a player is at 0.

On their turn, a player throws 3 darts and subtracts the total of their points from the remaining score. The last dart must usually land in a double (“double out”) to finish at 0. If a turn would take you below 0, or leave 1 point (impossible to finish on a double), the turn is cancelled and the score stays what it was.
Each turn, enter in the player’s column the total of their 3 darts. The app shows the remaining score, and automatically ignores a turn that would go below 0 or to 1.
Knock down as many pins as possible over 10 frames. The maximum score is 300 points (12 strikes in a row).

In each frame, you have 2 rolls to knock down the 10 pins. A strike (X) is when all the pins fall on the first roll: you score 10 points plus the total of the next 2 rolls. A spare (/) is when all the pins fall in 2 rolls: you score 10 points plus the next roll. Otherwise, you score the number of pins knocked down.
A player who gets a strike or a spare in the tenth frame is entitled to one or two more rolls, for a maximum of 3 rolls.

Tap a frame’s cell and enter the number of pins knocked down on each roll. The cell shows the frame’s notation (X, /, -) and the running score, which appears once the bonus rolls are known. The game ends when the 10 frames of all the players are entered.
Finish the course with as few strokes as possible. The player with the fewest strokes at the end wins.
At each hole, each player counts their number of strokes to put the ball in the hole. Over 9 or 18 holes, you add up the strokes of all the holes.
Each row of the table is a hole: enter in each player’s column their number of strokes. Rows are added automatically. The standings put the player with the fewest strokes first.
Be the first to reach 11 points with a 2-point lead. The app ends the game when a player has at least 11 points and leads by 2: at 10-10 it keeps going until someone leads by 2.
Add (+1 / −1) a point to the player who has just won the rally. The serve changes every 2 points.

Be the first to reach 21 points with a 2-point lead, up to a maximum of 30. The app ends the game when a player has at least 21 points and leads by 2, or as soon as someone reaches 30 (at 29-29 the next point wins).
Add (+1 / −1) a point to the player who has just won the rally.
Be the first team to reach 25 points with a 2-point lead (15 in the deciding set). The app ends the game when a team has at least 25 points and leads by 2.
Add (+1 / −1) a point to the team that has just won the rally. To track sets, play one set per game.
Be the first to score 10 goals. The app stops the game as soon as a player or team reaches 10.
Add (+1 / −1) a goal to the player or team that has just scored.

A Portuguese trick-taking game for 4 players, in two teams of 2 (partners sit opposite each other), with 40 cards: a 52-card deck without the 8s, 9s and 10s. The first team to reach 4 game points (a “partida”) wins. The app stops the game as soon as a team reaches 4 points.

The order of the cards, from highest to lowest, is: ace, 7 (the “manilha”), king, jack, queen, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. Card points: ace 11, 7 10, king 4, jack 3, queen 2, the other cards 0. Each suit is worth 30 points, i.e. 120 points in the whole deck.

Each player gets 10 cards. The dealer shows their last card: its suit is trump. 10 tricks are played: you must follow suit if you can, otherwise you play any card (you may trump). The trick is won by the highest trump, or failing that by the highest card of the suit led. Partners must not tell each other their hands.

At the end of the deal, each team counts the points of the cards in its tricks. More than 60 points: 1 game point. 91 points or more: 2 game points. A team that wins all the tricks (“dar uma bandeira”) scores 4 points and wins the game. At 60 against 60, nobody scores (depending on the table, the next deal is then worth one extra point).

At the end of each deal, enter in the column of the team that won the deal 1, 2 or 4 game points (0 for the other team). You can play with 2 columns (the two teams) or with 4 players. Some regions play to 6 points instead of 4: in that case, carry on the game by hand.

This poker tournament is played with chips: everyone starts with the same stack. A player with no chips left is out; the last player standing wins. The app does not deal cards: it keeps track of chips, bets and the order of play.

The button moves one player along every hand: the player to its left posts the small blind, the next one the big blind. With two players, the button posts the small blind. Blinds go up at regular intervals (the new level applies from the next hand). If antes are on, every player pays one on every hand.

In turn, a player can fold, call (or check when there is nothing to call), raise or go all-in. A raise must be at least as big as the previous one (at least the big blind). After a raise, all the other players must act again. An all-in smaller than the minimum raise does not let players who already acted raise again. At showdown, pick the winner of each pot (main and side pots); in case of a tie, the pot is split.

To merge two tables: export the players of the table that is closing to a file, then import that file on the other table. Players arrive with their stacks and sit at random between the players already there, without changing their order or the dealer button.
Remove these players from this table after exporting
Can\'t remove these players: at least two players must remain in contention at this table. To close this table, export everyone without removing them, then leave the game.

Attract the most birds to your three habitats (forest, grassland, wetland) over four rounds, then count your points. The highest total wins.

Add up: the points printed on the birds you played, bonus cards, end-of-round goals, eggs (1 point each), food on cards (1 point each) and cards tucked under birds (1 point each). With the Oceania expansion, add the nectar majority points of each habitat.
At the end of the game, enter in each player\'s column the total of each family of points, one family per row.
A cooperative game: the whole team builds fireworks, colour by colour, by playing cards from 1 to 5 in order. Everyone sees the others\' cards but not their own.

The score is the sum, for each colour, of the highest card played (0 to 5). It is at most 25 with five colours, 30 with the rainbow colour. Reading the score: 0 to 5, horrible, the crowd boos; 6 to 10, mediocre, hardly any applause; 11 to 15, honourable, but it will not be remembered; 16 to 20, excellent, the audience is delighted; 21 to 24, extraordinary, the crowd is amazed; 25, legendary, stars in their eyes.
One column for the whole team (rename it as you like). One row per colour: pick the value of the highest card played. Leave the rainbow row at 0 if you do not play that variant.
Sum of the points printed on the birds you played.
Points from your bonus cards, according to what they ask for.
Total points from the four end-of-round goals.
1 point per egg on your birds.
1 point per food token on your cards.
1 point per card tucked under a bird.
Oceania expansion: in each habitat, 5 points for the most nectar spent and 2 for the second most. Leave empty without the expansion.
Value of the highest card played in this colour (0 if none).
Rainbow variant: same principle. Leave at 0 if you do not play this variant.

Tricks needed to make this contract: %1$d.
Contract %1$d · Overtricks %2$d · Part-score or game bonus %3$d · Slam %4$d · Double bonus %5$d
“Open” implies Hand, Schneider announced and Schwarz announced.
Bid too high: the game is lost.
Announcement not made: the game is lost.

Bridge is played by 4 players in two partnerships of 2 (North-South against East-West). After the bidding, one side commits to a contract: a number of tricks (6 + the level, from 1 to 7) with a trump suit or in no trump. The defenders try to defeat it.

The app uses duplicate (tournament) scoring, deal by deal. Contract made: points for the contract tricks (20 a trick in clubs and diamonds, 30 in hearts and spades, 40 then 30 in no trump; doubled if doubled, quadrupled if redoubled), plus overtricks, plus a bonus: 50 for a part-score, 300 (500 vulnerable) for a game (contract worth 100 points or more), 500 (750) for a small slam, 1,000 (1,500) for a grand slam. Contract down: the defenders score a penalty for each undertrick (50 not vulnerable, 100 vulnerable, more if the contract was doubled).

The two “players” are the two sides (for example North-South and East-West). For each deal, choose the declaring side, the contract (level and suit), any double, the vulnerability and the tricks taken: the score is calculated and added to the right side. You can correct or delete a deal in the history. Rubber bridge (with honours and scoring above the line) is not supported.

Skat is played by 3 players (or 4, with the dealer sitting out) with 32 cards. One player, the declarer, plays alone against the others: they choose a suit game (clubs, spades, hearts or diamonds), a grand (only the jacks are trump) or a null (they must take no tricks).

In a suit game or grand, the game value is its base value (clubs 12, spades 11, hearts 10, diamonds 9, grand 24) multiplied by: 1 (the game) + the matadors (“with” or “without” 1 to 11) + 1 for Hand + 1 for Open + 1 for Schneider announced + 1 for Schwarz announced + 1 for Schneider made + 1 for Schwarz made. Null has a fixed value: 23, Hand 35, Open 46, Open Hand 59. Tournament list scoring (Seeger-Fabian): game won, 50 + the game value; game lost, −(50 + 2 × the value) for the declarer and +30 for each of the other players. A bid higher than the game value, or an announcement that is not made, loses the game.

For each deal, choose the declarer, the game, the matadors, the options (Hand, Open, announcements) and the result: the game value and the scores are calculated. The bid is optional: enter it to catch a bid that was too high. Ramsch is not supported.
Settings can no longer be changed once the first point is played.
Win the match by winning the required number of sets (2 in a best of 3, 3 in a best of 5). A set is won at 6 games with a 2-game lead; at 6-6 a tie-break to 7 points (win by 2) decides the set (7-6).

Points are counted 15, 30, 40, then game. At 40-40 (deuce) you need a 2-point lead: the first point gives the advantage, the next one the game. The deciding set can be played with a tie-break at 6-6, with a super tie-break to 10 points, or with no tie-break (2-game lead).

Choose the format before the first point, then tap the button of the player or team that wins the rally. The app counts points, games and sets, switches to the tie-break and announces the winner; “Undo” removes the last point. The first players in the list form the first side (in doubles: the first two against the last two).

Padel is played in doubles (two teams of two). As in tennis, you win the match by winning the required number of sets (usually 2 in a best of 3); a set is won at 6 games with a 2-game lead, or by tie-break at 6-6.

In padel the golden point is often used: at 40-40 the next point decides the game, with no advantage. The app turns it on by default for padel; you can turn it off before the first point. In casual play the deciding set is often replaced by a super tie-break to 10 points.

Choose the format before the first point, then tap the button of the player or team that wins the rally. The app counts points, games and sets, switches to the tie-break and announces the winner; “Undo” removes the last point. The first players in the list form the first side (in doubles: the first two against the last two).

Be the first to reach 200 points. The game ends at the end of the round in which at least one player reaches or passes 200; the highest total wins. If players are tied for the lead, play one more round.

On your turn, draw a card or stay. Number cards go from 0 to 12. Drawing a number you already have in front of you makes you bust: you score 0 for the round, unless you have a Second Chance. Action cards (Freeze, Flip Three, Second Chance) and modifier cards (+2 to +10, ×2) are mixed into the deck. The round ends when nobody is still playing, or as soon as a player collects 7 different numbers: a “Flip 7”.
Add up your number cards; the ×2 card doubles that total, then the +2 to +10 modifiers are added. A Flip 7 is worth 15 extra points. A player who busted scores 0.
At the end of each round, enter each player’s score (0 for a player who busted). The app adds the rounds up and ends the game at the end of the round in which a player reaches 200.
Tap a die to keep it before rolling again.
Roll the dice to see the possible scores.
Tokens to give: %1$d. Choose the player:

Each player creates a secret sequence of colors. All the sequences are searched at the same time: one attempt at player 1’s sequence, then one at player 2’s, and so on, before starting again with the first. The players whose sequence it is not agree on the attempt. The winner is the player with the lowest average number of attempts.

The players who are searching agree on a combination, then submit it. The app answers with two numbers: pegs of the right color in the right place (well placed, black dot) and pegs of the right color in the wrong place (misplaced, white dot). The sequence is cracked when every peg is well placed; the number of attempts is limited.

For each player, the app averages the attempts it took to crack the sequences they searched (their own is not included). A sequence that was not cracked counts as one more attempt than the limit. The lowest average wins; with 3 or more players, that means having created the hardest sequence to find.

Choose the settings (pegs, colors, attempts), then everyone enters their sequence while passing the phone around. Each color carries a number, so you can recognize it without seeing it. After that, the phone keeps moving: each turn, the app says which sequence it is about. Tap a black or white dot to see what it means.
%1$s, choose your secret sequence. Everyone else, look away!
Average attempts to crack the sequences each player searched (their own is not included): the lowest wins.
The Mastermind game in progress will be lost.
Tap a black or white dot to see what it means.
Black dot: well placed peg, the right color in the right place.
White dot: misplaced peg, the right color but in the wrong place.
Two phones with this app can follow the same game, with no internet and no Wi-Fi network to join: Bluetooth and direct connection are used automatically. What one phone enters shows up on the other.
To host a game, start one first from the home screen.
This game (poker, tennis, padel) can’t be shared yet.
